speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner for the second reading of Bill No. C-190, to amend the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act.

maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a question of privilege. This arises as a result of something which came to my attention late last evening. During the debate on Bill No. C-190 on February 12 as reported at page 6851 of Hansard I stated that chloramphenicol manufactured in the United States by nine companies had been allowed back on the market after rechecking. My information, Mr. Speaker, was incorrect. These products have not been allowed back on the United States market. I apologize to the house and express my appreciation in particular to the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) for drawing this matter to my attention.

maintopic: PATENT ACT-TRADE MARKS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING IMPORTATION OF PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking last evening I tried to stress the point that we in the official opposition agree with the stated objectives of this bill. However, we have grave concern on two main points. The first is the almost impossible task facing the food and drug directorate in attempting to assure the safety and quality of drugs for Canadians, if the drugs are easily imported from other countries without adequate supervision. Second, we are concerned that the legitimate pharmaceutical research in this country may be needlessly but seriously hindered and reduced as a result of this bill in its present form. With regard to the first point, I should like to quote a telegram which was received this morning from the president of the Canadian Medical Association. It is addressed to the president of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, with a copy to the Prime Minister and others, and reads as follows:
Re Bill C-190; further to our previous communications to the Hon. John Turner on this subject the Canadian Medical Association continues to be deeply concerned that Bill C-190 in the form now being presented to parliament may open the door to drugs whose safety and effectiveness are below the standard expected and deserved by the Canadian public. Although we too favour the availability of drugs at a lower cost we are not convinced that the implementation of Bill C-190 will accomplish 

this end and we fear that the more important factors of safety and effectiveness may be compromised.
Our concern is not restricted to the importation of generic drugs. We fear that confusion may arise due to the importation of brand name drugs some of which have ingredients, physiological activity and dosage forms different from similarly named Canadian brands.
Under present government requirements quality control is responsibility of the drug manufacturer under the supervision of the food and drug directorate, Department of National Health and Welfare. Under this new legislation allowing the importation of drugs it will be extremely difficult if not impossible for the food and drug directorate to maintain the same degree of supervision over foreign manufacturers.
We urgently request that this bill receive further detailed study and necessary amendments to provide adequate safeguards for the public. The association stands ready to aid in any such investigation.
Dr. N. J. Belliveau, President, Canadian Medical Association
Since coming into the house I have received another telegram which is brief but,
I think, very important because it comes from a large Canadian owned drug manufacturer which I think specializes in generic drugs. This telegram is addressed to myself and reads as follows:
As a major Canadian owned pharmaceutical enterprise Empire Laboratories is vitally concerned with consequences of Bill C-190. Contrary to statements by bill's advocates, bill seriously threatens existence of Canadian owned segment of drug industry. Moreover the public health is threatened. Food and drug directorate cannot possibly ensure every import is manufactured under sanitary conditions-
And so on. With regard to the second point, I should like to point out that during the course of this debate I have heard various supporters of the bill say a great many times that the pharmaceutical industry has earnings which are twice as high as those of the average industry in the country. However, at page 12 of its report the committee says: Your committee believes this to be true for pharmaceutical companies generally, whether they be so called "innovators" or "copiers"; or brand name or generic producers. It should be pointed out in all fairness (as seen in table 4 of the appendix E), that the pharmaceutical industry showed (in 1963) the seventh highest rates of return on resources employed, and are exceeded by distilleries, wineries, motor vehicles, petroleum and coal products, motor vehicle parts and accessories, wire and wire products, and office and store machinery.
So there is a wide range of activity here in which the new minister can indulge. With regard to the pharmaceutical industry, it is my belief that they are good corporate citizens generally speaking, and I believe they
February 14, 1968

would welcome negotiation or discussion with the Department of Consumer Affairs with regard to prices, advertising and guide lines which might be set down which would have the effect of reducing the cost of drugs to the consumer.
It seems to me that the government in drafting this bill has flailed about with a bludgeon in a situation where the deft use of a scalpel is what is required. We in the official opposition hope that the minister will see fit to withdraw the bill from committee of the whole and refer it to a suitable committee to bring it more into line with the recommendations of the special committee, while preserving its position on the order paper.
If the minister does not accept this suggestion, we in the official opposition expect that he will have the bill suitably amended or will agree to suitable amendments in committee of the whole on the points I have stressed, so that the public interest will be safeguarded. We of course reserve our position with regard to third reading until the final content of the bill is established by the committee of the whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the previous speaker in this debate I shall be very brief. It is possible for me to be very brief because hon. members who have spoken in the debate in the last few days have gone into the technical aspects and ramifications of the bill in great detail. I was greatly impressed with the contributions made to the debate by those hon. members who are of the medical profession; in particular, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), my colleague the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) and the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Isabelle). I listened closely to what was said by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and then read his speech in Hansard.
With respect to the reasons which have been advanced by members of the official opposition who are opposed to the bill, I find myself completely unconvinced by their arguments. The two main arguments put forward in opposition to proceeding with this bill, as I gather from listening to them and then reading the speeches in Hansard, are that while the legislation shall bring into the Canadian drug market a greater degree of price competition, it will somehow lead to a deterioration of quality control and will make it more difficult to maintain high standards of drug safety.
They also make much of the argument that if the profit of drug companies is reduced their capability to conduct research and development will be lowered. In advancing these arguments hon. members apparently failed to take account of some obvious facts. First, as was shown clearly by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley), drug safety inspection can be taken as a fact. It must be policy on the part of any government to see that medicines and drugs put on the market, regardless of price, measure up to certain criteria or standards of safety. Any attempt to relate price to drug safety is spurious and illogical.
February 14, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
In respect of the argument that any reduction in the margin of profit will encourage a greater degree of price competition in the industry and lower the capability of that industry to undertake research and development, let me point out that the industry spends about four and a half times as much on promotional advertising as it does on research and development.
If research and development is a prime function of the industry, as it ought to be, there is nothing in this legislation which will reduce the capability of the industry to engage in research. The industry may have to cut back on its promotional activity but, as has been suggested by several hon. members, particularly those of the medical profession, there seems to be a proliferation on the part of the industry to seduce the medical profession, through the use of a great number of brochures and advertising gimmicks. As has been said, many doctors in this country feel the time has long passed when material emanating from the pharmaceutical manufacturing houses serves any useful purpose. Much of this material is consigned to the wastebasket. All this promotion increases the expenses of the firms, which they pass on in good measure to the consumer.
Let me refer to one other point which was brought forward by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). He took exception to what the minister sponsoring this bill said about the inclusion of those charts which were appended to Hansard for Monday, and which indicated that the price of drugs in Canada was much higher than in most other industrialized countries.
That hon. member suggested that these charts were misleading because they do not take into account the relative purchasing power and wage scales in these other countries where drug prices are considerably lower than in Canada. The hon. member was obviously suggesting that since wages or incomes are lower in these countries, the price of drugs should be lower. Apparently he feels there can be some reason for higher drug prices in Canada if only because of higher incomes. While there may be some validity to the argument, the hon. member has ignored one essential point.
The pricing practice used by pharmaceutical houses is obviously divorced from production costs and the cost of research. Obviously their pricing practice is not related to the cost of production as it should be, but rather to some judgment as to what the market will


bear, or what the Canadian consumer will pay without complaining too much. The differential between costs and selling price is enormous. The practice over the years has been to increase the price little by little over a period of time. Whenever it is felt there is imminency of consumer price complaint, the increases are stopped.
I suggest that if it were not for action of responsible public bodies such as parliament, this practice would likely continue. Many interesting pieces of information were brought to light in evidence presented to the committee on drug costs and prices, and by evidence presented to two other investigating bodies. Inasmuch as much of this information has been aired and discussed in this chamber,
I feel I would be serving no useful purpose in referring to it again.
Let me conclude by saying there is no question but that there is a direct and obvious responsibility on this government and parliament to pass this legislation, even though, taken by itself, it may not have a great impact. Together with other measures the minister has indicated this government is contemplating, this measure will have the effect of bringing drug prices in this country down to levels which can be justified by the cost of production and research. I wish to commend the minister and his colleagues for the enlightened and bold position they have taken which was not really expected.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank hon. members of the house for allowing me to close the debate at this time, so that the bill may go to the committee of the whole for further discussion and elucidation, particularly in respect of some points referred to in general terms during this debate on second reading.
Let me deal briefly with those points referred to by hon. members on all sides of the house, particularly the chief spokesman for the official opposition, the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard). He suggested that the bill was confiscatory in that it took away property rights of patentees under the Patent Act. I assure hon. members that I listened to his point with the greatest interest.
February 14, 1988
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I want to say to the hon. member in general terms that this bill does not, to use his words, virtually abolish patent protection. In effect, a five year monopoly under the patent is maintained because of the period that elapses under the present food and drug regulations, and thereafter the patentee, if there is a compulsory licence issued, will enjoy the protection he has gained through establishing a position in the market. This is a position he would enjoy under ordinary circumstances for five years under the patent. In addition, he will enjoy the royalties from any new rivals who may have been able to obtain a compulsory licence from the patent commissioner. This is not confiscation of property, Mr. Speaker, because what we are doing here is diluting, to a certain extent, the patent protection in a way that is analogous to reducing a tariff.
The purpose of this bill is to reduce the effect and use of a patent as an analogous economic weapon, if you will, to the tariff. I may say that the domestic drug industry will still obtain the 15 per cent most favoured nation tariff. Both the patent and the tariff are economic institutions that are designed to achieve particular economic ends. I want to say to the hon. member, through you, Mr. Speaker, that much research, innovation and invention is not patentable. I want to say also to the hon. member that patent laws vary widely around the world according to the needs of the individual economies. A patent right is not an absolute right. It is a right that has to be weighed in the balance of economic convenience. In this case, it is the objective of the bill to weigh the legitimate rights of the Canadian consumer against the legitimate rights of the inventor and the drug industry. In this sense, this bill moves Canada closer to the position already adopted by the United Kingdom and the United States.
Many members were worried about the fact that this bill, if carried by the house, would have an effect on employment. In my opening speech, sir, I recited the figures relating to the people employed by the drug industry in this country. It is my view, on the basis of the best advice I was able to obtain, that this bill will not adversely affect employment within the drug industry in Canada. About 85 per cent of the Canadian drug industry converts the basic chemical ingredients from their basic form into final dosage form, that is to say into the pill, the tube or syrups. This
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act bill, if effective, would introduce more competition into that manufacturing process. It should not affect the amount of manufacturing done in Canada. It would tend to make manufacturing more competitive, but the amount of employment should not be affected to any degree.
Some members were disturbed by the possibility of Canada importing large amounts of drugs from Italy, Hong Kong and other parts of the world. Here again, I want to remind the house, if I may, that 85 per cent of the Canadian drug manufacturing industry in Canada really exists on importation of the basic ingredients, and conversion of those basic ingredients into the final dosage form. We already import 85 per cent of the basic chemicals into Canada. We do not expect this bill will unduly rearrange this percentage.
Then, some members were concerned, and perhaps I would share their concern if I were criticizing this bill, about the possibility of research in Canada being adversely affected by this measure. It is our view again, sir, and I hope I was able to make this point in my opening speech, that patent protection by itself is not an inducement to research. We have had patent protection in this country ever since confederation.
Until very recently only three major drug companies did any appreciable research in Canada, and the increase in research done in this country was probably attributable more to direct government intervention by way of research grants and tax incentives than it was by virtue of the patent system. The existence of a patent, therefore, is not the sole reason for research being done here. I hope that government programs for research within the competence of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) would amply encourage the continuance of whatever research in drugs is done in Canada.
I think the house ought to recall that the drug industry is an international industry. All the major companies having 85 per cent of the business in this country are controlled abroad, either in the United States, Switzerland, the United Kingdom or some other country. When these international concerns, subsidiaries and related companies in various parts of the world decide where they are going to put research, they will put research where the market is or where available scientists can be found.

In most cases, research has to be concentrated in one place because of the highly complicated, highly specialized nature of the research and because of the expensive equipment needed to mount it. Not very much of the international research done in the drug industry has found itself resident in Canada. There is nothing in this bill, to our mind, which would promote the changing of the location of research in Canada, if that research were otherwise economically desirable here.
Finally, I want to deal with a point that seemed to be occupying the minds of most speakers who had the courtesy to enter the debate, and that is the question of safety. I was particularly impressed by the learned address by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) last evening, as well as the very respected member for Queens (Mr. MacLean). They dwelt particularly on this subject.
I want to say again that, regardless of the economic motives for this bill, that is to say, to provoke more competition, to encourage more free enterprise, to encourage competition in price rather than merely in a promotional sense, there are two other objectives. As I said at the outset, the first of these objectives is to maintain safe, efficacious, high quality drugs in Canada. There is no doubt about that. I want to restate my concern and the concern of the government on that score. The second objective is to maintain a viable domestic drug industry.

I want to get back to safety, Mr. Speaker. A number of hon. members expressed concern that the bill did not contain what they referred to as adequate safeguards respecting quality and safety of drugs. I would emphasize what I said previously, Mr. Speaker, namely that in the government's program designed to reduce the price of drugs, the need to supply the Canadian market with safe and efficacious drugs is paramount. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I refrained from speaking diming the second reading stage, thinking it would be better if I spoke when the house is in committee. Many hon. members in the debate spoke at length about the drug industry and about the price of drugs. I do not intend to speak about the necessity for immediate measures to reduce the price of drugs. That this necessity exists was fully demonstrated in the committee chaired by the hon. member for Halton.
I am satisfied that the price of drugs is excessive and that that is harmful to the economy and to the nation. I am also satisfied it has been proven that the safety and quality of drugs is not related to ownership or control of patents, or to the products of a few brand name firms. On the contrary, it is well known that certain licensees of patent owners have produced better quality drugs than the so called ethical or brand name firms have produced. I am also satisfied that a large proportion of the profits which are accumulated by our pharmaceutical industry, so called,, which is foreign owned, reverts to foreign hands.
In view of recent legislation which has been enacted in many provinces and by the Canadian government, under which medical and hospital care would become a responsibility of government, I have become particularly worried about the cost of drugs. It has been said that over 30 per cent of medicare costs will be attributed to drugs and pharmaceutical products. Unless effective legislation is introduced, this country could price itself out of any scheme which will provide the medical services that it wishes to extend to its citizens. The United Kingdom met this difficulty by importing its drugs directly from Switzerland and other countries. Under its medicare plan these drugs are distributed at a very low cost.
This bill, Mr. Chairman, deals with amendments to the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act. In passing, I wish to say that it is unfortunate that we are still dealing with the old Patent Act eight years after the royal commission made a report on patents to this house. Nothing has been done since then. Had something been done we should not now be
February 14, 1968

faced with the difficulties that we are faced with.
The minister has already indicated that this bill is only one step in a larger program which is to effect a reduction in drug prices. Owners of patents should realize that they are beneficiaries of a monopoly extended to them by parliament. In effect, that monopoly gives them unlimited latitude to fix prices for their products, and to control their distribution. There has been little investigation into this feature of patents. Furthermore the house knows that the term of a patent, which is for 17 years, is much longer than necessary under modern conditions.
True, certain clauses in the Patent Act which relate to compulsory licences deal with abuses, but it has always been most difficult, or almost impossible, to make a case of abuse before the courts, because of the great litigation costs in appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada, and because the relevant sections of the act are not strong enough.
In the case of patents on drugs, a great body of opinion has held that patents should not be granted for medical products and foods. Italy is one country which has subscribed to this view. I do not intend to take sides, but I venture the opinion that at the present time our large brand name firms will do as well without patents as they now do with patents, so long as they have their present unlimited resources for publicity, advertising and soliciting, and so long as they have the co-operation of the medical profession, the members of which find it easier to order drugs by their trade names instead of by their generic names.
I remind the committee also that 95 per cent of our Canadian patents are held by foreign firms that the control, distribution, quality and availability of drugs lies in their hands.
I now wish to say a few words about the legislation. In my view it is very fair legislation. It is a fact that foreign firms which hold patents in Canada have the right to import drug ingredients-sometimes they import the finished product-from their parent companies. The legislation which has been submitted to this house gives that same right to an approved importer who is other than the subsidiary of the owner of the patent, except that any new licensees will have to pay royalties. Such licensee must satisfy the food and drug directorate and must find a market for his product in the face of stiff competition. He will have to satisfy the food and drug
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act administration that his product is satisfactory from the point of view of safety and quality.
I should like to pay tribute to our own food and drug directorate. I remind the committee that though we do not follow the United States practice, which is to publish the results of investigations and court cases, it might be a good idea to do so. Hon. members may be surprised to learn that investigations are not always direced against the so-called-and I do not know whether this is the correct term to use-disreputable companies. Somebody said that some firms which are not reputable are selling drugs. To make that suggestion is not to pay a compliment to our food and drug administration.
If the results of investigations were published it would be found that even the so-called brand name firms have been looked into. They are just as likely as other firms to produce products which are not of good quality or approved purity. The fact that a firm overprices its drugs gives us no guarantee of the quality of those drugs. True, certain sections in the Patent Act relate to compulsory licensing and to abuses but, as I have said, those abuses are hard to prove.
Not too many firms can afford the cost of the proceedings that are involved in obtaining a licence, and very few licences will be certified by the food and drug directorate. That is why this legislation will create little problem for those who sympathize with the large companies. Licences must be approved by the food and drug directorate. Firms seeking those licences must have money to obtain them and money to compete with firms which are already established.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
This legislation will at least give a chance to Canadian firms to get established, in the hope of developing a Canadian pharmaceutical industry providing drugs at a competitive price. The large patent owners have only themselves to blame for this legislation. They have consistently refused licences to reliable small firms, while at the same time they have willingly licensed some of their large competitors so as to restrict the market and control prices. This is one feature which I believe should be investigated in greater depth by the combines branch.
A great deal has been said about research to be carried out by some of the large firms in Canada. I am satisfied that very little research is being carried on, in comparison with the benefits which accrue to some of the
February 14, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act larger firms. As a matter of fact, the few discoveries we have made in the field of drugs in Canada can be attributed, not to these firms but to government agencies, universities or hospitals. A great deal of the staff involved in research comes from these sources, and the money comes from governments.
I repeat what I said earlier about the term of life of patents for drugs. I consider that a term of 17 years is far too long. It has been my experience that the commercial use of a drug patent is from five to seven years after which, for many reasons, including economic ones, a substitute is developed under a new brand name. There are some doctors present in the committee and they should know this to be true. I know it to be the case. There is the example of librium, which came out a few years ago. It had a real life of only some four or five years before it was superseded by a tranquilizer which was stated to be much better-and of course it was-namely valium. This is why I do not like the provision for a fixed five-year term in connection with the refusal of licences.
I should like to say a word about applications for licences. I am sure the minister realizes that the commissioner of patents has very heavy responsibilities and that he will not be able to hear many applications in one year. The minister should assure the committee that he will be provided with the necessary power and staff to enable applications to be heard by a properly constituted board, say three or four men, otherwise the delays will be endless.
I am against appeals to the Exchequer Court from these decisions. Under the legislation with which we are dealing, decisions by the commissioner are always followed by appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada and the cost of such appeals is excessive. Some hon. members have drawn attention to the fact that under the present practice only a few applications for compulsory licences have been heard in past years. This is the reason, and it is easy to understand. I speak as a patent lawyer. I never could find a client who was in a position to drag litigation out for four or five years culminating in hearings by the Supreme Court of Canada, to be faced in the end, possibly, by a bill of costs which could run to $7,000, even if I did not charge him one cent.
I shall not say much about the trade mark provisions in this bill, except to remind the committee that the most important protection


afforded to brand name firms is the trade mark under which they sell their drugs. As long as the medical profession insists on prescribing by brand names, and if governments do the same, there is really no other protection required in order to maintain the status quo.
Mr. Chairman, I hope this legislation will achieve the desired result. But this will happen only if there are enough competent and approved applicants for licences. In any event we must remind ourselves of the fact that any reduction in prices would also be within the power of the licensee. How much will that be?

speechtext:
I should like to make a few further observations on Bill C-190. I have already placed on record my views with regard to the question of patent rights, and I have described what might be the effect of these provisions on the drug industry. I have expressed the view that the main requisite when prescribing drugs is safety-that drugs should be safe, and able to do the clinical job which they are supposed to do. I have put on record what the granting of patent rights has done for the Connaught medical research laboratories at the University of Toronto.
I doubt whether any of this research could have been carried out in the absence of patent rights with respect to insulin. The number of employees there now is about 800. Sales alone amount to more than $6 million, and the export trade to just under $2 million. But the value of the work this laboratory has done is immeasurable. I could cite the names of many professional people engaged in research who are able to continue to carry out work of great value to mankind, as a result of the discovery of insulin and similar drugs. Because their lives were saved they were able to carry on with some of the most fruitful work which has been done in the University of Toronto area. Whether one thinks of all this in the terms of the suffering which has been relieved or in the economics of dollars and cents, the benefit is beyond measure. I do not think for one moment we should disregard these aspects in a country of 20 million people. When insulin was discovered, our population numbered only 10 million. Yet the discovery was made here in Canada, and nowhere else in the world.
It has been stated disparagingly that the drug industry puts only 7 per cent of its budget into research. I want to ask you this, Mr. Chairman: What does industry generally put into research? What do other industries
February 14, 1968	COMMONS
in Canada devote to research? The figure in the case of the drug industry is higher than that of any other industry in Canada. This is a state of affairs that we must preserve. Do the people of Canada want to pay for all their research to be done in the United States or some other foreign country, as it is done today for many Canadian subsidiaries? I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that it cost us well over $300 million last year for research done in the United States-a lot of it by people who were educated in this country; we paid the cost of their education and then they went to the United States because research jobs were not available here. What a folly that is. As I have said previously, the cost of educating a medical doctor is well over $50,000. Are we going to let that go as an asset to some other country because we do not provide doctors with facilities for research in Canada? This is folly of the worst sort. The same applies to pharmaceutical research.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
When our young doctors go to the United States they become American citizens. Not so long ago I was in Boston, where I met three young Canadian doctors who had been educated in this country. Consider the cost of raising them, paying the baby bonus, paying for their education, putting them through medical school, giving them three or four years training afterwards, and then consider that they went to the United States because that is where the opportunities for research are. They did not have the opportunity to do research in Canada.
Last year the drug industry in Canada poured $12 million into research. I will not say this bill will destroy our drug industry, but I wish to indicate what has happened in other fields. The government takes the attitude that so much of our drug industry is owned outside Canada that the rest does not matter. I ask how much of the oil industry and of the manufacturing industry is owned outside Canada?
How are we ever going to build a country if we do not keep our university educated young men and women in Canada? At present they are going to the United States. I could name Canadians who are top flight men not only in research but in every other field in the United States. I wonder how many hon. members know that last year we paid over $300 million to the United States for industrial research. Surely we cannot build up a country by doing things like that.

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act
All of us want cheaper drugs, cheaper food, cheaper automobiles and lower rents. It does not faze the government, but we also want lower taxes. Our cost of living is at an all time high and I have not heard any suggestions about what the government will do in that regard. True, the government wants drug costs lowered. I am in favour of that 100 per cent, if the safety of drugs is protected. But what is the government doing about the cost of living and about high taxes? These are the things that make us non-competitive in many fields of production.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is smart. I think he is flexible, and I hope he will not be arrogant when it comes to making some amendments to this bill. He has a nice smile. He certainly leads you to believe that he is going to go along with you. I really like him, but I know he has to pilot a bad bill through this house and I sympathize with him. I hope he will show that elasticity and good judgment which will go across Canada to show the people that not only is he concerned about their getting cheaper drugs, but also that he is concerned that the drugs they get will do the job they are supposed to do. In the final analysis we will expect to make this a good bill.
One of the things which has struck me about the government, and this is something I said the other day, is that it allowed foreign imports of boots and shoes to increase year after year, until they pretty nearly put the Canadian boot and shoe industry out of business, a business which, per dollar, employs more people than most other industries. At present about 6 per cent of our labour force is unemployed. The rate of unemployment is going up and up like an escalator, but the government is not protecting the drug industry.
The same thing applies to the textile industry, and this really bothers me because there is a textile plant in my constituency. It is not a big plant by United States standards, but if the government does not move to abolish textile dumping, on July 1, 1968 foreign manufacturers will be able to dump more textiles in Canada in one month than all of our own textile firms could produce. The result will be more and more unemployment.
The same thing applies to farming. What is the government doing about the dairy industry? More and more people are being forced out of dairying with the result that we will have to buy more and more dairy products from other countries. I could also speak about
February 14, 1968

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act the fruit and vegetable industry. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce said we have to be competitive. How can we be competitive in the drug field, or in any other field, when workmen in some other countries are being paid a third of what Canadian workmen receive? Does that make common sense? The result will be to put Canadian workmen out of jobs. We cannot have the second highest standard of living in the world and import all foreign goods. Look at our balance of payments situation.
Now the government is sponsoring this bill even though its spokesmen have said they do not know what its ultimate effect will be. They hope it will not be disastrous; but this government has done so many things that were disastrous that naturally I am a bit suspicious.
I now wish to deal with the comparative prices of drugs. Many tables which I think are not too relevant have been published during the course of the debate on this bill. I think the hon. lady from Grenville-Dundas put it very clearly when, as recorded at page 6702 of yesterday's Hansard, she said:
We have heard a great deal about the possible savings that can be made by using generic as against brand name drugs. An independent company, International Surveys Limited produced a report dated November 27, 1967 on its investigation of the relative cost of prescriptions written under brand names compared with those under generic names. The basis for the selection of drugs to be studied was as follows: they had to be well established, they had to cover as wide a range as possible in different therapeutic fields. Controlled drugs and drugs restricted by the Narcotics Act were excluded from the inquiry.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Major cities across Canada were chosen for use in the survey and pharmacies were selected at random from the yellow pages of telephone directories.
In the 11 categories of drugs studied, the differences in cost between brand and generic prescriptions were found to be negligible in nine of the categories. In one category the price of generic drugs was significantly higher and in one other the brand name prescriptions were significantly higher in price. The differences in price as between one outlet and another were found to be considerable.
I believe that is very true of the situation across Canada.
I was interested in what the hon. member for Winnipeg North had to say. I listened to him and I read his speech, and it was not too clear to me what he meant. However, I believe he said that the hospitals across Canada used generic drugs. I should like to say that I am not deriding generic drugs; there 

are some very good generic manufacturers. There are generic drugs which have been tested clinically and which have come up to standard. However, to come back to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North said, or what I thought he said, I checked with 12 hospitals across Canada today and found that they do not use generic drugs: They use brand name drugs. I was advised by one of the hospitals that they had at one time purchased other generic name drugs, but they found that it was necessary to test them clinically and that after testing many of them did not come up to the standards they required in the treatment of their patients. They found that the cost of testing was too high and therefore discarded the idea of buying other than brand name drugs.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. As I was saying, it cost Parke, Davis about $5 million to research that drug. Their patent rights lasted for 17 years. It was a valuable drug, was most often used in cases of very serious illness. Last December those patent rights ran out. In January or February of 1967 five other companies applied for and obtained a compulsory licence to manufacture the drug chloramphenicol. These companies were granted this right, manufactured the
6736	COMMONS
Patent Act-Trade Marks Act drug and marketed it. Parke, Davis continued manufacturing it also. Around June doctors started to note that they were not getting the results from chloramphenicol that they should have been getting; it was not doing the job. They started to check up in hospitals and found that Parke, Davis' chloramphenicol was doing the job and the blood levels were all right. In the case of the drug manufactured by other companies, the blood levels were at various levels and urinary output in respect of the drug varied as well.
The point with any life saving drug, or any drug used when a patient is acutely ill, is to get the blood at such a level that the components of the drug in the patient's blood are strong enough to kill the germ that has attacked the patient. Therefore the drug is life saving. I do not know whether some people died in the United States as a result of the use of the drug chloramphenicol; I did not go into all the facts. But as a result of the investigation, all those drugs manufactured under compulsory licence were recalled from the market by the food and drugs department of the United States. Chloramphenicol as produced by Parke, Davis is the only such drug one can purchase today in the United States. I thank the hon. member for Halton, the chairman of our committee, for stating that he had ascertained that the information I have given to the committee is correct. I appreciate that very much.
This is the important point. You had a drug that met exactly the requirements of the food and drugs department of the United States. It met those requirements in every detail. A compulsory licence was granted for the manufacture of the drug, but clinically the drug failed. I say to the minister that this is one of the points that must be written into this bill, namely the clinical efficiency of the drug; because nothing else matters.
The drug can be safe as far as the components are concerned, but it is not necessarily clinically efficient. We have a great example of this right now with respect to Parke, Davis. I am sure the Prime Minister will look into this matter immediately. I asked him about it today during the question period. You can go downtown in Ottawa and buy chloramphenicol of different brands. I do not think this is good enough or smart enough. I do not think this should be the situation.
I point out to the minister that, leaving out other factors that may also be of great importance, the factor of greatest importance is the

clinical efficiency of the drug that will save somebody's life, instead of losing it. Once the organism or the germ gets ahead of the antibiotic and is not being controlled, you may lose your patient. I again say to the minister that this is something the medical profession demands above all things, namely that the drug doctors are using be clinically efficient.
Somebody said this is an emotional matter. If you have ever sat by the bedside of somebody fighting for his life, and you have been checking the blood level and checking the patient clinically, hoping and praying that the drug would make the blood level high enough to kill the organism or germ, you would know that this is not an emotional matter. Anybody who brands it as emotional should not be in the house; he is not mature enough to be here.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, this should be a prime consideration in the bill. Every doctor, every patient, has the right to be assured of clinical efficiency in respect of the drugs he uses. I will have more to say on this subject when we deal with other clauses of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I want to enter this debate very briefly to clarify a misunderstanding which arose during the second reading debate. I did not take part in that discussion; neither was I a member of the committee, though I read the committee reports.
I must confess that as I listened to the discussion during the second reading stage, instead of becoming more enlightened I became more confused. I became confused about the minister's purpose in introducing this legislaton at this time. The bill itself is described as "An Act to amend the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act". That sounds like something a lawyer might concern himself with. Matters involving patents and trade marks seem to occupy the attention of the legal beagles in the house. Those who have not that professional background are not so preoccupied with such matters.
It seemed to me, after listening to the minister's speech the other afternoon and reviewing it in Hansard, that he was talking about a bill which would lower drug prices in Canada. That need not necessarily have anything to do with the Patent Act or the Trade Marks Act. Nevertheless the minister kept emphasizing all the wonderful things that this legislation would accomplish in terms of lowering drug prices in Canada. As father of a large family, I say that that is a consummation devoutly to be wished. We all agree that the problem of health care in Canada is aggravated by high drug prices. Unfortunately none of the multiplicity of welfare and health programs on our statute books at the present time has done anything to deal with that problem.
As I listened to the presentations of other hon. members in the house I had the impression that the actual effect of this bill would be to threaten an important industry of Canada and lower the quality of pharmaceutical products. I was impressed by the leading spokesman of this party when he spoke on second reading the other day. I thought he summarized the legislation logically, and concluded by recommending that since there is much confusion about this bill, as expressed in the various viewpoints in the house, it might be wise to send it to a committee for further consideration so that this confusion might be clarified.
This afternoon the minister indicated that he had had representations from many groups outside the house and advice from hon. members in the house. I can only conclude that if
February 14, 1968	COMMONS
he has received such representations, he has not read them carefully. From my reading of those representations, I thought some important and legitimate points were made.
One reason that I wish to speak at this time is that I was impressed by the presentation last evening of the hon. member for Jacques-Cartier-Lasalle. Since he spoke from the government side of the house it is obvious that he has no partisan axe to grind. He spoke from the standpoint of quality and safety of drugs, a viewpoint that has emerged in several speeches, and also about the threat that this legislation poses to the continuing health and progress of an important part of our industrial complex. The hon. member I thought spoke with authority, representing an area which has located in it a substantial part of our pharmaceutical industry. He brought information before the house, read from letters and mentioned names, and I think he persuaded the minister that it might be wise to follow the advice of the hon. member for Simcoe East and recommend that this matter be referred to a committee.
The minister says that the purpose of this bill is to lower drug prices. It is impossible to demonstrate at this juncture whether that can be done. Also we do not seem to be sure of the end result of the legislation; it has been suggested that one effect will be the lowering of quality of drugs and the endangering of the Canadian pharmaceutical industry. It has been my experience in the house that when an important item of legislation which will have a multi-pronged impact and which is full of uncertainties and imponderables is introduced, the course of wisdom dictates that we should be allowed a further opportunity to sort out any confusion that has arisen. That confusion has arisen was demonstrated in the debate on second reading.
Unhappily we have gone beyond the stage where this matter can be referred to a committee. We are now in the committee of the whole stage. Nevertheless I shall make one final plea this afternoon. If we are to avoid some of the potential dangers which have been outlined, the minister may wish to move amendments to the bill. The necessity for those amendments has been demonstrated to him, and I think he is convinced that they are necessary. I saw him nodding his head during the course of the debate as various points were raised. I think he is convinced that the legislation, as it stands, will not necessarily accomplish its objectives. Certainly, it will have some unforeseen effects which have been pointed out by other hon. members.

second state is indeed going to be worse than our first.

By this bill we are adding another almost impossible task to its responsibilities. However, the minister did point out that in the long run the quality of drugs depends on the integrity of the manufacturers. I agree with him.
We can be assured of the best quality drugs only when we deal with reputable manufacturers. I am sure that by far the greatest number of drug firms operating in Canada are in that category. They are here to serve the public to the best of their ability, to give them the best quality medicine for the treatment of disease and illness. They are not out to exploit the public in any shape or form.
If the situation be otherwise, then as I have already indicated the combines investigation machinery should be put to work; but the minister should not try to create a smokescreen through the sort of legislation we have before us. As one who is concerned about the state of the economy and the prospects for expanding industrial development in all parts of Canada, I am concerned about the suggestions that have been put forward by several hon. members, that if this legislation is arbitrarily imposed upon the Canadian drug industry it will mean a decline in that industry.
This legislation could add to the brain drain. I have received one or two letters-I will not put them on the record-from individuals, specialists in the field of research in Canada, who have written to say that if this legislation is passed they will have no other alternative but to join the brain drain, as we call it, that treks regularly across the border into our neighbour to the south, where opportunities for research are already much more plentiful than they are in Canada.
I think the minister is a responsible person.
I know he is seeking even greater responsibility. If he wished to demonstrate to the people of Canada that he is serious in his current ambitions, now that he has refused to send the bill to a standing committee I trust he will seize the initiative and bring forward amendments to the bill which will remove beyond shadow of doubt the possible bad side effects mentioned by several hon. members when they spoke about safety, quality, and the impact of the bill on the drug industry.
